articles.title: Roman lifts off on a mission to survey the infrared sky
articles.description:
Image:
			
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA, at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST/ 13:26 CEST on 30 August 2026. With the successful launch, Roman began its mission to survey the sky in visible to near-infrared light to help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter. The telescope will also investigate the true diversity of exoplanets in our galaxy.
Roman is a NASA-led mission to which the European Space Agency (ESA) contributed star trackers, batteries, and detectors for the coronagraph instrument. ESA will also provide communications support through its deep-space ground station network, and enable data download using its new 35-metre antenna in New Norcia, Australia.
“I warmly congratulate our colleagues at NASA on the successful launch of Roman,” says Carole Mundell, ESA’s Director of Science. “ESA is proud to have provided essential hardware and to continue supporting Roman’s ambitious scientific goals. Together, we are opening new windows on the cosmos.”
Like ESA’s Euclid space telescope, Roman will enable astronomers to study the Universe in unprecedented detail. It is equipped with a primary mirror of 2.4 m and two instruments: the Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration.
With its panoramic view of the sky, crisp infrared vision and quick re-orientation skills, Roman will perform fast and efficient surveys of a large area of the sky. By doing so, it will map clustering of galaxies over time and space and also study the light coming from thousands of distant type Ia supernovas which will help astronomers trace the expansion of the Universe.
“Roman should provide our clearest picture yet of whether dark energy is truly constant or whether it evolves over cosmic time – either outcome would have profound implications for our understanding of the Universe. I'm also excited by Roman's exoplanet census, which will discover thousands of new worlds, including cold planets and free-floating planets that have remained largely beyond our reach until now,” says Bethan James, ESA’s Roman Project Scientist. “Perhaps what excites me most is the unexpected. With its unprecedented combination of depth, area, and image quality, Roman has every opportunity to surprise us.”
After launch, Roman is on a steady course to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), nearly 1.5 million km away from Earth. This location allows the telescope to have an unobstructed view of a wide area of the sky, almost 12%. Like ESA’s Euclid and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, Roman will move in a wider orbit around the L2 point – much larger than the Moon’s orbit around Earth.
In the next three months following launch, the Roman team will conduct a carefully orchestrated series of deployments, calibrations, and tests. Once the commissioning period is complete, the mission will begin its science operations, starting with the first science image release. Roman will spend at least five years scanning the infrared sky and is designed to work in space for another five years.
[Image description: A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on board is seen transiting the Sun during launch from Launch Complex 39A, on Sunday 30 August 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, US.]
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket to conduct a transformative infrared survey of the cosmos.

articles.title: Watch live: BepiColombo begins its arrival at Mercury
articles.description:
After eight years, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission is about to enter its Mercury Arrival Phase. On 3 September 2026, ESA’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from BepiColombo’s two science orbiters – the first major step in one of the most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.  
The European Space Agency (ESA) will livestream the critical milestone from 13:45 CEST. Tune in and witness the first step of one of the most complex phases of the mission, live from ESA mission control.  
Join ESA's livestream on YouTube here!
articles.summary: After eight years of travel, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission reaches its Mercury Arrival Phase, beginning unprecedented exploration of the closest planet to the Sun.

articles.title: Cutting-edge infrared space telescope Roman set to launch
articles.description:
The NASA-led Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch on 30 August 2026 at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST / 13:26 CEST from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA.
With its wide field of view and advanced optical design, the Roman telescope will conduct detailed scans of the sky in visible to near-infrared light. In doing so, Roman will help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter and find new exoplanets.
articles.summary: The cutting-edge Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch on August 30, 2026, beginning its mission to revolutionize infrared astronomy.

articles.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope launches to reveal the Universe’s darkest secrets
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has launched on a million mile journey to L2, where it will scan huge portions of the cosmos for clues about dark matter, dark energy, and distant worlds. With survey speeds roughly 1,000 times faster than Hubble and a torrent of 1.4 terabytes of data per day, Roman could uncover cosmic surprises astronomers have never seen before.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope has launched to the L2 point to survey vast cosmic regions and unlock mysteries of dark matter and dark energy, representing a landmark observatory for modern cosmology.

articles.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has launched into orbit to revolutionize our understanding of the universe through unprecedented observations of galaxies and exoplanets.

During its five-year primary mission, Roman is expected to observe billions of stars and galaxies, 100,000 exoplanets, and more.

articles.title: NASA’s powerful new Nancy Grace Roman Telescope begins cosmic mission
articles.description: NASA's new flagship astronomical observatory was launched into space from Florida on August 30 on a mission to probe some of the biggest mysteries in astrophysics and cosmology. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a roughly $4 billion project, was carried …
articles.summary: NASA's powerful Nancy Grace Roman Telescope launches on an ambitious mission to probe the cosmos and advance our understanding of the universe.

articles.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope observes a giant, evolving, 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole.
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope discovers a remarkable 10-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn's south pole, revealing dynamic planetary weather patterns.

articles.description: NASA awarded Blue Origin a contract Tuesday to develop the agency’s Mars Telecommunications Network, a next-generation communications system that will enable reliable, high-bandwidth communications and navigation services for current and future Mars missions. The firm-fixed-price contract has a maximum potential value of approximately $700 million to deliver a high-performance Mars telecommunications orbiter to NASA no […]
articles.summary: NASA selects Blue Origin to develop a next-generation Mars Telecommunications Network, advancing humanity's communication capabilities for future Mars exploration.

articles.title: Fly around Schiaparelli Crater with Mars Express
articles.description:
Video: 
			00:04:10
				
ESA’s Mars Express takes us on another mesmerising flight, this time around one of the biggest craters on Mars. 
Despite measuring a huge 460 km across, Schiaparelli Crater seems to be relatively shallow. Perhaps it has been filled in over the last few billion years by sediment blown by the wind or deposited by water, by lava – or by a combination of all three. 
Schiaparelli Crater is named after Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli (1835–1910). Although he studied Mercury and Venus, he is best known for his observations of the Red Planet. 
During the ‘Great Opposition’ of 1877, when Mars passed close to Earth, Schiaparelli mapped the planet, perceiving several straight dark lines across the red surface. He assumed that these were natural water-filled channels and used the equivalent Italian word, ‘canali’. 
However, other astronomers thought he meant canals, meaning artificial irrigation and transportation routes, which led to a few astronomers, and a large number of the general public, believing that they had been created by intelligent martians. 
Now we know that Schiaparelli’s ‘canali’ were illusions created by the comparatively poor telescopes of the time and there are no water-filled channels on Mars today. Nevertheless, we do believe that water was once present in this region of the planet, perhaps in the form of a lake. 
Schiaparelli Crater is also important in popular culture, being the final destination of astronaut Mark Watney in Andy Weir’s novel ‘The Martian’. 
Enjoy the flight, and be sure to turn up the volume for the full audio guide experience. 
 
Processing notes: 
This film was created using the Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera Mars Chart (HMC-30) data, image mosaics made from multiple observations by the mission’s High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC). The mosaic image, centred at 8°S/17°E, is combined with topography information from the digital terrain model to generate a three-dimensional landscape. 
For every second of the movie, 50 separate frames are rendered following a predefined camera path in the scene. The vertical exaggeration used for the animation is three-fold. Atmospheric effects, like clouds and haze, have been added to conceal the limits of the terrain model. The haze starts building up at a distance of 250 km. 
The HRSC camera on Mars Express is operated by the German Aerospace Center (DLR). The systematic processing of the camera data took place at the DLR Institute for Space Research in Berlin-Adlershof. The working group of Planetary Science and Remote Sensing at Freie Universität Berlin used the data to create the film.
articles.summary: ESA's Mars Express captures stunning video footage of Schiaparelli Crater, one of Mars's largest impact features. The mesmerizing flyover provides detailed views of the Martian surface and crater geology.

articles.title: Physicists Determine Cause of "Runaway" Supermassive Black Hole
articles.description: Researchers at UCSB and UT Austin have determined that a galactic merger kicked a supermassive black hole into intergalactic space.
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered that a galactic merger can eject supermassive black holes at tremendous velocities. This breakthrough helps explain the mysterious phenomenon of runaway supermassive black holes traveling through space.

articles.title: SuperCDMS SNOLAB Starts Its Dark Matter Hunt
articles.description: The search for dark matter has reached another milestone - in this case the start of science for one of the world’s newest detectors. The Super Cryogenic Dark Matter Search (SuperCDMS) SNOLAB just began its scientific operations in Ontario, and over the course of the next few years, hope to find direct evidence of “light” dark matter for the first time.
articles.summary: The SuperCDMS SNOLAB experiment has begun its science operations as one of the world's most sensitive dark matter detectors. This milestone represents a major step forward in the decades-long quest to directly detect dark matter particles.

articles.title: Distant Quasars Provide Crucial Link In Understanding Earliest Supermassive Black Holes
articles.description: Extreme quasars near the dawn of time are giving astrophysicists clues to the formation of supermassive black holes.
articles.summary: Distant quasars from the early universe are providing crucial insights into how supermassive black holes formed in the cosmos's infancy. These extreme objects offer a unique window into black hole formation mechanisms.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn's south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving, 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn's south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large, regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet's southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn's famous hexagon at its north pole but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon developing on the iconic gas giant.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope has discovered a giant 10-sided atmospheric wave pattern encircling Saturn's south pole. This striking geometric feature reveals fascinating dynamics in Saturn's atmosphere.

articles.title: Young sunlike system reveals comets may carry water toward forming planets
articles.description: Astronomers at Lund University in Sweden have found evidence of exocomets—comets in other solar systems—orbiting a young star similar to our sun. The observations point to a possible mechanism for how water might be transported from the cold outer regions of the planetary system to regions where planets form.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered evidence of exocomets orbiting a young sunlike star, suggesting that comets may deliver water to forming planets. This finding illuminates how habitable worlds acquire the water essential for life.

articles.title: More than 120 molecular species found in giant cloud near Milky Way's center
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered a second interstellar cloud near the center of the Milky Way that is extraordinarily rich in complex molecules, including several molecules associated with prebiotic chemistry. The newly studied cloud, G+0.633-0.0604, or G+0.633, contains more than 120 identified molecular species and is the first confirmed chemical twin of another famous molecule-rich cloud. Their paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 14, outlines the chemistry of the newfound cloud.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered an extraordinarily rich interstellar cloud near the Milky Way's center containing over 120 molecular species. This remarkable discovery deepens our understanding of complex chemistry in the galactic center.

articles.title: Earth may have lost the Sun’s protective shield millions of years ago
articles.description: NASA-funded studies suggest Earth’s climate has been influenced by both the Sun’s travels through dense regions of the Milky Way and the violent superflares of its youth. Those events may help explain ancient ice ages as well as how early Earth stayed warm enough for liquid water when the Sun was much dimmer.
articles.summary: NASA-funded research suggests Earth's climate has been shaped by the Sun's passage through dense regions of the Milky Way, revealing profound connections between galactic dynamics and planetary protection.

articles.title: This strange “spacetime crystal” can suddenly become a black hole
articles.description: Physicists have mathematically captured a bizarre “spacetime crystal” that can either dissolve or collapse into a microscopic black hole after only a tiny change in energy. Their breakthrough came from an unusual trick involving infinitely many dimensions, potentially giving researchers a new tool for studying primordial and microscopic black holes.
articles.summary: Physicists have theoretically discovered a remarkable 'spacetime crystal' that can transform into a black hole, expanding our understanding of exotic spacetime geometries and quantum gravity.

articles.title: Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
articles.description: Rocky planets may have been able to start forming just 100 million years after the Big Bang, thanks to enormous early supernovae that scattered planet-building elements across space. Simulations found enough solid material and water around a young star to suggest that Earth-like worlds could have appeared far earlier than previously believed.
articles.summary: New research reveals that rocky planets may have begun forming just 100 million years after the Big Bang through massive early supernovae, pushing back the timeline of planetary genesis.

articles.title: 2 spacecraft headed to Mercury are about to begin their long-awaited arrival for Europe and Japan — watch it live on Sept. 3
articles.description: The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission will begin its drawn-out Mercury arrival phase on Sept. 3, and you can watch the action live.
articles.summary: The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is beginning its long-awaited arrival phase at Mercury on September 3, promising groundbreaking observations of the solar system's innermost planet.

articles.title: Blue Origin wins $700 million contract to build NASA's next Mars orbiter
articles.description: NASA has picked Blue Origin to build its next Mars telecommunications orbiter, awarding a $700 million contract to Jeff Bezos' spaceflight company.
articles.summary: NASA has awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract to build an advanced Mars telecommunications orbiter, advancing human exploration capabilities for future Mars missions.

articles.title: Supermassive black holes 'too big' for the early universe may not be so massive after all
articles.description: Over massive supermassive black holes too big for early galaxies and detected by the James Webb Space Telescope may not be quite so massive after all.
articles.summary: James Webb Space Telescope observations of supermassive black holes in the early universe may have been misinterpreted, suggesting these objects aren't as massive as previously thought and resolving a cosmological puzzle.

articles.description:
SETI@home’s 12 billion threshold events became roughly 100 FAST follow-up targets after interference filtering, blind synthetic-signal tests and manual review.
The post For 21 years, millions of volunteers let UC Berkeley use their home computers to search th…
articles.summary: Two decades of SETI@home data from millions of volunteer computers identified approximately 100 promising targets for extraterrestrial signal searches after filtering 12 billion candidate detections.

articles.title: Radio telescopes have accumulated petabytes of observations originally used to map galaxies and black holes—but no one had searched those archives minute by minute for activity from every star in view. In 2026, a new algorithm reprocessed 1.4 years of LOFAR data and uncovered eight faint bursts from low-mass stars that conventional images had missed, including signals potentially produced by magnetic interactions with orbiting planets.
articles.description:
RIMS recovered eight intermittent M-dwarf radio bursts from archived LOFAR measurements, including one suggestive but unconfirmed star-planet signal.
The post Radio telescopes have accumulated petabytes of observations originally used to map galaxies and blac…
articles.summary: A new algorithm discovered eight faint radio bursts from low-mass stars in archived LOFAR telescope data, including signals potentially caused by magnetic interactions with orbiting planets.

articles.title: On January 27, 2025, asteroid 2024 YR4 crossed the 1% impact-probability threshold; two days later, the International Asteroid Warning Network sent its first-ever formal asteroid warning to the UN’s space office—activating a planetary-defence protocol created more than a decade earlier but never previously used.
articles.description:
Asteroid 2024 YR4 became the first object to trigger IAWN's formal UN notification protocol, testing a warning system whose successful end point was an all-clear.
The post On January 27, 2025, asteroid 2024 YR4 crossed the 1% impact-probability threshold; two…
articles.summary: Asteroid 2024 YR4 became the first object to trigger an international planetary-defense protocol, successfully testing a decade-old warning system designed to protect Earth.

articles.title: Rising Over Louisiana
articles.description: On Aug. 28, 2026 (the evening of Aug. 27 in some time zones), the Moon passed into Earth’s shadow, creating a deep partial lunar eclipse. At the moment of greatest eclipse, 12:13 a.m. EDT, 96.3% of the Moon’s disk was immersed in Earth’s umbra—the central, darkest part of the shadow where sunlight is completely blocked. […]
articles.summary: The Moon passes through Earth's shadow in a partial lunar eclipse, offering skywatchers a spectacular celestial event.

articles.title: NASA Rocket Takes First Multi-Point Look Inside Radio-Disrupting Clouds
articles.description: High above Earth, thin veils of metallic haze drift through the edge of space. Known as sporadic E layers, these high-altitude “clouds” form from the vaporized dust of burnt-up meteors, earning their name from the unpredictable way they emerge and then dissipate. Now, new results from a NASA sounding rocket — a suborbital research rocket […]
articles.summary: A NASA rocket conducts groundbreaking multi-point observations of sporadic E layers, high-altitude metallic clouds at the edge of space.
